doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Producing Miles Davis and Miles Ahead
summary: He signed Miles while under Prestige contract, got him Jack Whittemore, the 1955 quintet, Gil Evans and the Miles Ahead cover.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: In your career as a producer, did you have a philosophy about when you approached a new artist you hadn’t worked with before about how to produce them?

Yes. The basic idea was very, very simple. How can I help the artist present himself in the most effective way for his benefit as well as of course the company? But in many cases there was a matter of what do you do to make the artist appealing to the potential record customer, and most of the time the artist had no idea except that man I just want to blow you know. And that’s why it became important as everything grew more and more competitive to find ways of presenting artists, including jazz artists, in a way that will stand out. One of the classic examples of course is Miles Davis because Miles was constantly performing with small groups, quintet, sextet, and the music was more or less of the same except for the variety within it, and when I signed Miles I had a very strange problem. Miles persuaded me to sign him while he was still under contract to Prestige Records, because he was dying to get on Columbia, where he knew that he would get a lot more exposure. And he finally convinced me that he was not only off the drugs and so forth and was becoming reliable, which he certainly wasn’t to the extent that he had no manager, he had no booking agent who would really work seriously with him because he was considered so risky. I realized that the way to handle it is to figure out a program whereby we could record him for a year and a half without permission to release him because of his contract with Prestige. They allowed us to do that, a very unusual contract. And how could he keep on working and building himself up to the point where he would mean something when we were able to launch him on the label. And the solution was to convince Miles that he should try to form a group that could stick together and even though that group would primarily record for Prestige, I would able to record it also. And to hold it together he needed management. He had a manager who was really a friend of his, but he needed a strong booking agency, and I got him Jack Wittemore, who was with the Shaw Artists Agency, and I told Jack if Miles can form a group and you can hold it together, I think we can really do something when he’s on the Columbia label. And that’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

what happened. Miles was fortunate enough to get the original quintet together very quickly in September ‘55. I went to hear them for the first time in Philadelphia when he called and said, “Hey, I’ve got these terrific guys: Coltrane— and Coltrane was just a name to me, I’d never even heard him — Philly Joe Jones and Paul Chambers and Red Garland, well I knew them of course. And he did hold them together and Wittemore did do a terrific job of booking them when there were no Columbia records to back them up so that when we got the first album out “Round Midnight” — which commemorated the performance of the song at Newport — I’d already told Miles before that release look we’ve got to do something different. And of course Miles was just interested in getting out and playing. And that’s how the idea of Gil Evans’ arrangements came about. And the title of the album, I told Miles and Gil is going to be “Miles Ahead,” so give me an original composition, we’ll make a DJ single of that and some of the other selections because the album as you know, is done as a complete suite, continuous. So for DJs we had to put out the separate singles. And I told the art director the album is going to be called “Miles Ahead,” what can you give me as a cover that will say Miles is ahead of everybody else and Miles is moving ahead, he’s miles ahead of everything. And he came up with that sailboat photograph, which he’d got from an agency which tells the story, you look past the girl and the sailboat, she’s miles ahead of everybody, there’s nothing but blue sky and blue ocean behind her, she’s winning the race. She doesn’t look like she’s racing but she’s attractive. And that whole promotion worked like a dream. That album sold unbelievably and established Miles all over the world. Miles hated the cover of course because it was a white girl.
Well it’s a pretty astute balance of artistic and commercial concerns.
